newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, U.S. settle bitter row over Okinawa bases.
newsitem.headline: Japan, U.S. settle bitter row over Okinawa bases.

text.p: The United States and Japan on Monday settled a bitter dispute over U.S. military bases, agreeing to reduce the U.S. presence on Okinawa and announcing tentative plans for a revolutionary floating helicopter base.

The agreement, announced by the Japanese Foreign Ministry, was signed by U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry and other top U.S. and Japanese officials, culminating a year of intense negotiations spurred by the September 1995 rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.

The U.S. military will return a fifth of the 58,000 acres (23,500 hectares) it now uses on the island and close part or all of 11 facilities there. It will also reduce aircraft noise, but keep all of the 28,000 American troops now on Okinawa, 1,000 km (650 miles) southeast of Tokyo.

The two countries agreed to close the Futenma Marine Corps Air Station in the densely populated city of Ginowan in five to seven years and to make plans to build a 1,500-metre (yard)-long floating helicopter base somewhere off the east coast of the island at an expected cost of more than $2 billion to Japan.

"The United States and Japan will seek to build a sea-based facility -- a creative solution using advanced basing concepts -- to absorb most of the helicopter functions at Futenma Air Station," the announcement said.

Japan had not decided the exact location of such a floating base, but the two countries said a detailed implementation plan, including an assessment of its environmental impact, would be drawn up within a year and that Futenma would be returned after adequate replacement facilities were completed.
The highly visible and noisy presence of the U.S. military on Okinawa has for decades drawn "Yankee Go Home" protests from islanders.
Those objections rose to a fever pitch after the rape of a 12-year-old schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen on Okinawa 14 months ago.
The three were convicted in a Japanese court and are serving up to 10 years in a Japanese prison.

The agreement, including key changes in Marine Corps training and flight operations, was finalised on Monday in a meeting between Perry, U.S. Ambassador Walter Mondale and Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda and Defence Minister Fumio Kyuma.
The bases issue has been one of the most contentious between Washington and Tokyo since World War Two.

Perry told reporters travelling with him that the agreement would reduce the U.S. military intrusion on the lives of Okinawans but would not diminish U.S. security in either Okinawa or elsewhere in Japan.
The agreement would make no cuts in the overall total of 47,000 U.S. troops in Japan.
Okinawa was the site of bitter fighting between U.S. and Japanese troops near the end of World War Two, and was governed by the U.S. military until Washington handed the island back to Japan in 1972.
